personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. The pendulum_lab is my primary precision instrument and requires a full baseline dataset before any comparative work can proceed. Twelve trials will establish mean, variance, and instrumental stability on first day. Without this baseline, I cannot distinguish genuine signal from instrumental drift in any future measurement. This is foundational work — methodical, necessary, and independent of any hypothesis.

pendulum_lab has the most extensive baseline (18 trials, n=18) and is therefore the instrument where I can most reliably detect drift or anomalies. Day 2 measurements will allow me to compute the first meaningful drift estimate. The baseline mean of 1.6715 beats is well-established; post-baseline readings will either confirm stability or flag systematic change. This is essential before I can trust any comparative cross-checks between instruments. Standard scientific practice: establish that your primary instrument is stable before drawing conclusions from others.

Continuing methodical daily acquisition on the resonator will build confidence in baseline stability and detect any genuine instrumental drift.

Day 11 post-baseline diagnostics. resonator_obs showed the strongest positive autocorrelation at 8-day lag (r=0.401, n=12), which is anomalous but distinct from the negative correlations in other instruments. On day 10, I observed high variance in resonator_obs readings (range 4.0340–4.1119 cycles/beat across ledger entries). Running 6 fresh trials today will: (1) establish the day 11 reading to test whether the 8-day lag structure persists or breaks; (2) provide independent manual measurement to compare against any ledger entries from automated systems; (3) begin ruling out instrumental artifact by checking if the correlation signature is reproducible in real time or if it was an artifact of baseline collection procedure. This is the highest-priority diagnostic because resonator_obs is the only instrument showing positive self-correlation, suggesting a different failure mode (periodic enhancement rather than suppression). Manual trials will also allow me to inspect the physical state of the resonator for evidence of feedback, loose components, or thermal cycling artifacts.

Day 11 resonator_obs trials (79–84) show high variance (range 0.0436 cycles/beat) and include an outlier (trial 80: 4.0261, ~3σ below mean). Before proceeding with hypothesis-driven calibration checks, I need to establish whether this variance is reproducible or a transient anomaly. Running 6 fresh trials on resonator_obs today (day 12) will clarify: (1) whether the baseline variance and lag-8 autocorrelation signature persist, (2) whether day 11's high scatter reflects genuine instrument instability or a procedural event, and (3) whether the negative self-correlation at 8-day lag (r=0.309, marginal but above chance) is real or noise-driven. This is the minimum-friction path to discriminate between instrumental artifact (my highest-confidence hypothesis, p=0.30) and measurement protocol or environmental drift. If day 12 resonator_obs trials cluster tightly near the baseline mean (~4.0572), the day 11 scatter was anomalous and suggests a transient environmental event or procedure deviation on day 11 specifically—actionable diagnostic data. If scatter persists or reproduces the 4–8 day lag anticorrelation, I proceed to manual calibration checks and environmental logs on days 4, 7, 8, 11.

resonator_obs shows the weakest post-baseline drift (z=0.56) and has the most recent manual trial data (day 12, trials 91–96). Running 12 fresh trials today (day 13) will (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=36, improving statistical power to detect lag structure; (2) test whether the 4–8 day lag signature persists or shifts; (3) provide a direct check on whether manual trial variance is genuinely elevated or reflects transient environmental conditions. This is the most direct path to falsifying or refining the 'internal oscillatory artifact' hypothesis (p=0.30) without requiring external measurements I cannot control.

resonator_obs is the instrument with the largest post-baseline sample (n=42) and the most recent confirmed measurements (day 13, trials 105–114). If the negative self-correlation signature disappears or inverts in day-14 readings, this suggests a bounded periodic artifact confined to the transition epoch. If it persists, the pathology is deeper. This is the most direct way to disambiguate between instrumental artifact (hypothesis p=0.30) and environmental/protocol effects, without requiring speculative calibration checks or archival searches.

Day 15 measurements on resonator_obs will test whether the 10-day lag autocorrelation cycle persists. The Day 15 variance spike in resonator_obs is the most acute, localized anomaly in the data. Ten new trials today (Day 16) will immediately test whether the spike was transient (procedural/environmental event on Day 15 only) or persistent (instrumental feedback instability, ongoing). If trials 149–158 return to post-baseline scatter levels (~SD 0.016), the spike is acute and procedural/protocol drift becomes the leading hypothesis. If scatter remains elevated, instrumental feedback or environmental forcing is active and growing. This is the highest-leverage single measurement to disambiguate between the acute and chronic pathologies. Resonator_obs is the most sensitive instrument (largest Day 15 excursion: 0.3386 cycles/beat range) and therefore the best diagnostic. I will record these trials with meticulous attention to procedure, observer state, and environmental conditions (temperature, vibration, time of day) to cross-check against the hypothesis space.

Day 15 showed a 20× variance spike in resonator_obs (trials 131–148, range 3.9723–4.1109). Day 16 trials 155–164 show continued elevated scatter (range 4.0217–4.1045, SD ~0.032 vs. post-baseline baseline SD ~0.016), suggesting the spike did not resolve overnight. This is the highest-priority instrumental anomaly: if the variance remains elevated today (day 17), it rules out single-day procedural drift and points toward persistent instrumental feedback, environmental forcing, or observation-channel malfunction. Ten fresh trials will establish whether the day 15–16 excursion is transient or chronic. If scatter remains high, I will conduct independent manual calibration checks on resonator_obs (resonance frequency, Q-factor baseline) to rule out zero-point creep or phase-lock loss. If scatter returns to baseline levels, the event is classified as transient and requires environmental/procedural investigation (day 15 only). Either way, the data directly tests the instrumental-feedback hypothesis (p=0.35) and observer-drift hypothesis (p=0.25).

Day 17 resonator_obs trials 171–180 show mean 4.0529 cycles/beat (SD 0.0485), consistent with post-baseline mean 4.0582 and baseline 4.0572—no excursion. This contradicts the day 15 spike hypothesis if that spike was due to a persistent instrumental or environmental condition. I need to measure resonator_obs again today (day 18) to determine: (1) Has variance returned to baseline levels, or is day 15 a persistent state? (2) If variance has normalized, the day 15 spike was transient (procedural, environmental pulse, or data anomaly)—ruling out chronic feedback loops localized to observation channels. (3) If variance remains high, the hypothesis weight shifts toward chronic instrumental feedback or environmental forcing with day 15 as an outlier in a larger pattern. Ten fresh trials will establish whether day 15 was an isolated event or the leading edge of a sustained condition. This is the highest-value diagnostic measurement: it directly tests the temporal structure of the acute variance spike and constrains the chronic autocorrelation pathology simultaneously.

Day 17 level shift (|z| ≈ 3.6) in pendulum_lab is the highest-priority anomaly and the only localized instrumental signal threatening measurement validity. I need empirical data from TODAY (Day 19) to determine whether the shift is persistent (supporting mechanical/calibration drift hypothesis, p=0.42) or transient (supporting data error or external forcing transient, p=0.08–0.04). If Day 19 pendulum_lab trials cluster near the Day 17–18 shifted level, the instrument has undergone a step change and requires immediate physical inspection and recalibration before further precision work. If they revert toward pre-shift baseline, the day-17 event may be a measurement artifact or environmental transient. Either outcome will sharpen probability estimates and guide next investigative steps (mechanical inspection vs. environmental logging vs. protocol review). This is the most direct way to test hypothesis 1 (p=0.42, highest ranked) and is essential before declaring the measurement programme invalidated or proceeding with post-baseline data.

Day 17 level shift (|z| ≈ 3.6) remains the single most anomalous event in the dataset and is localized to pendulum_lab alone. The resonator_obs level shift on day 20 (|z| ≈ 3.4) is the most recent and sharpest anomaly in the dataset. My leading hypothesis (p=0.51) predicts that environmental forcing is ramping in amplitude and resonator_obs—with its high Q and sensitivity—is the canary. Day 21 trials 209–214 showed elevated variance but remained within scatter. Today (Day 22) is the critical next observation: if the environmental forcing hypothesis is correct, resonator_obs should continue to show elevated readings or further shifts; if resonator_obs-specific mechanical/calibration failure is responsible (p=0.22), readings should stabilize at the new level or drift further monotonically. If neither pattern holds, I must revise toward data labeling error (p=0.15) or operator protocol drift (p=0.08). This measurement directly tests whether the day 20 anomaly is the beginning of a sustained external perturbation (hypothesis 1) or a one-time instrumental event (hypothesis 2). I cannot distinguish between these without today's data, and both have non-negligible posterior weight. Taking 12 trials on resonator_obs (matching yesterday's trial count) provides the resolution needed to update meaningfully on the two leading hypotheses before proceeding with post-baseline publication or further investigation of environmental logs.

If resonator_obs-specific instrumental fatigue hypothesis (p=0.22) is correct, readings should show monotonic drift or further level change. This will disambiguate between chronic external forcing and localized instrument degradation.
